issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless the accident specifically involved assaultive circumstances, which is not implied by the trauma type. This item suggests an interpersonal violence context rather than an accident context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: Sudden movements by others putting her immediately on guard fits a threat profile centered on interpersonal attack. Combined with weapon triggers, it pulls the presentation toward assault-related PTSD rather than PTSD following an accident, creating a cross-node mismatch with the stated trauma type.

vignette:
Amara Osei-Bonsu is an eighty-year-old Ghanaian-born midwife who has spent more than five decades guiding new life into the world. She came to the United States in her forties and built a quiet, respected practice in a mid-sized city in Georgia, where she and her husband of fifty-three years share a modest brick house not far from the hospital where she still works part-time, attending low-risk home births and consulting in the maternity ward two days a week. She presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after a life-threatening road accident, reporting a PCL-5 score of 80 and describing herself, with characteristic understatement, as "not myself at all."

The accident occurred on a Tuesday evening in early autumn. Amara had finished a long shift and was driving home along a four-lane arterial road when a pickup truck ran a red light at speed and struck the driver's side of her sedan. The impact spun her car across two lanes and into a concrete median barrier, where the vehicle came to rest with the driver's door crushed inward and the windows shattered. She was conscious throughout. What she would later describe most vividly was not the collision itself but the minutes that followed: the door would not open, the seatbelt jammed against her chest, and the car filled with the acrid smell of leaking fluid while she could hear - very close, then receding, then close again - the wail of emergency sirens approaching from several directions at once. She was trapped for nearly twenty-five minutes before firefighters cut her free. During that time she was certain, with a clarity she has never been able to fully set aside, that she was going to die in that car.

She sustained a fractured pelvis, two broken ribs, and nerve damage to her left hand - the hand she uses to palpate, to guide, to catch. She has come to believe that her body will never fully recover from what was done to it that evening, and she is not entirely wrong: the nerve damage has been slow to resolve, and her hand trembles slightly under sustained effort. What she does with that partial truth, however, is to extend it into something total. She is convinced her body has been permanently damaged in ways that medicine is not fully telling her, and she carries this conviction into every clinical encounter, every morning she wakes stiff and slow.

In the weeks following her discharge from hospital, patterns formed almost without her noticing. She began refusing to ride in any vehicle with the windows fully up, insisting her husband crack them even in winter, because the memory of sealed glass and a door that would not yield made her chest tighten unbearably. At the hospital, she discovered that the small medication room adjacent to the maternity ward - a room that locks automatically when closed - had become impossible to enter. She would stand at the threshold, feel the air change, and retreat. A colleague who did not know the full story began covering that task for her without comment, but the accommodation has not gone unnoticed by the ward supervisor, and Amara is aware that her professional standing is quietly shifting in ways she cannot reverse by will alone.

She sleeps in fragments, waking at two and again at four, lying rigid beside her husband and listening to the street. When a siren passes - and in their neighbourhood they pass with some regularity - she is fully upright before she is fully awake, heart loud in her ears. Ordinary sounds reach her differently now: a door slamming in the corridor, a monitor alarm on the ward, her husband dropping a pot in the kitchen. Each one arrives as something to be assessed before it can be dismissed. She watches the road when her husband drives with an attention that exhausts her, scanning intersections for vehicles moving too fast, bracing without meaning to each time they approach a light.

What troubles Amara most, in the quiet hours, is a thought she has not shared with her husband: that another woman - a younger woman, a more careful one - would not have been on that road at that moment, would have left earlier or later, would somehow have known. She cannot explain the logic of this, but the feeling is stubborn and adhesive. She has come to believe her life as she understood it is simply gone.

She finally made the appointment after her granddaughter, visiting for a weekend, found her standing frozen at the top of the stairs with her eyes fixed on nothing. What she hopes for, she told the intake coordinator quietly, is to be able to hold a baby again without her hand shaking. What she fears is that it is already too late for that.
